summary: Specifies rules for defining voucher properties in XML. A voucher is a logical entity representing a right to claim goods or services, such as coupons, tickets, loyalty points and gift certificates. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A coupon is a piece of paper that says you can get something. This memo describes a way to write down such coupons and tickets in a computer-friendly format.

questions: how to represent coupons in xml
subtitle: A standard XML format for describing coupons, tickets, and electronic vouchers

tldr.problem: Diverse applications need a common way to represent vouchers (coupons, tickets, loyalty points, gift certificates) with consistent semantics for issuance, transfer, and redemption.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4153 defines a Voucher Component structure in XML that specifies all properties a voucher needs: issuer, holder, value, merchandise, validity period, and conditions. It uses a modular architecture where different Voucher Trading System (VTS) implementations can be added as plug-ins to wallets.
tldr.outcome: Applications can exchange vouchers using a standard XML format, enabling interoperability between digital wallets, merchants, and issuing systems for various types of electronic value transfer.

facts.label: Spend attribute values
facts.value: 0 (reusable) or positive integer (number of vouchers needed)

today: RFC 4153 is an Informational RFC published in September 2005. It defines the syntax and semantics for voucher properties in XML, complementing the broader Voucher Trading System (VTS) framework defined in RFC 3506 and the VTS-API in RFC 4154.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC specifies rules for defining voucher properties using XML syntax. A voucher is a logical entity that represents a right to claim goods or services. Vouchers can represent many kinds of electronic values: coupons offering discounts, event tickets, loyalty points that accumulate when you shop, or gift certificates. They must be processed through a system that tracks their issuance, transfer among users, and final collection or redemption.

The RFC defines the Voucher Component, which encodes all the information a system needs to understand and process a voucher. A Voucher Component is not itself a voucher but a template: the issuer uses it to create many individual vouchers with the same properties. The document also assumes a modular architecture where different Voucher Trading Systems can be plugged in to wallets, allowing different security and implementation approaches.
sections.eli5: A voucher is like a coupon or gift card. The RFC defines how to write down what a voucher is, who made it, who can use it, what it is good for, and when it expires.

sections.title: How Vouchers are Processed
sections.content:
The RFC assumes a modular wallet architecture. When someone wants to use a voucher, the wallet software requests a Voucher Trading System (VTS) plug-in to handle the transaction. Instead of standardizing protocols for issuing, transferring, or redeeming vouchers (which would be impractical given varying security and deployment needs), the RFC standardizes two things: the Voucher Component format and the VTS API.

When sender and receiver agree on which vouchers to trade and which VTS to use, the issuing system or wallet requests the corresponding VTS plug-in to permit issue, transfer, or redeem transactions. The VTS then rewrites the ownership of the vouchers using its own protocol. Finally, a completion event is sent to the wallet and collecting systems. This design provides flexibility: different VTSes can use different security mechanisms (smartcard-based offline systems for coupons, centralized online systems for bonds), and all can coexist by supporting the same Voucher Component format.
sections.eli5: Your digital wallet can work with many different voucher systems, each with its own way of handling transfers and security. They all understand the same description of what a voucher is.

sections.title: Voucher Component Structure
sections.content:
A Voucher Component is an XML document containing the following elements. The <Title> and optional <Description> are simple text for display in wallet systems. The <Provider> element specifies or restricts which VTS Provider (or plug-in) can be used for trading the voucher. The optional <Issuer>, <Holder>, and <Collector> elements may contain authentication data or qualification information restricting who can issue, hold, or collect the voucher.

The <Value> element specifies the monetary or merchandise value. The optional <Merchandise> element describes what goods or services the voucher can be redeemed for. The optional <ValidPeriod> specifies when the voucher can be used (start date and end date). The optional <Conditions> element holds any other restrictions in natural language form. The <Value> element also has a spend attribute indicating how many vouchers must be redeemed to claim the value (for example, 10 loyalty points to get a reward, or 1 coupon).
sections.eli5: A voucher component describes: what it is called, who issues it, who can use it, what it is worth, what you can use it for, when it works, and any special rules.

sections.title: Value Types and Examples
sections.content:
The <Value> element has a type attribute that is one of three values. The exchange type means items in the <Merchandise> element can be claimed in exchange for the voucher (like redeeming a full-price ticket). The discount type means items can be purchased at a discounted price. The monetary type means the voucher has a fixed monetary value (a gift certificate or loyalty point worth).

When type is discount, the voucher contains either a <Ratio> element (specifying a percentage discount) or a <Fixed> element (specifying a dollar or other currency amount off). When type is monetary, it must contain a <Fixed> element with a currency code (like USD) and an amount. The <Fixed> element optionally includes a decimalPower attribute for precision, allowing amounts like 0.01 (one cent) to be represented.

An example: a five-dollar discount coupon for a specific book (ISBN 0071355014) valid from April 1, 2002, to March 31, 2003, redeemable by spending one coupon, with issuer Alice Book Center and VTS provider "Voucher Exchanger 2002".
sections.eli5: A voucher can be a straight trade (you give the coupon, you get the item), a discount (the item costs less), or money (you get a fixed amount off).

sections.title: Trust and Security
sections.content:
A voucher is trusted if the Issuer and VTS Provider are trusted. The issuer is responsible for the voucher's contents, and the VTS Provider is responsible for preventing ownership from being assigned to multiple users. The trust level required depends on the voucher type: a coupon may need less security than a bond or certificate.

The Voucher Component is the root of trust. If a malicious user alters it, a forged voucher could be verified as valid. When a Voucher Component is delivered, a secure communication channel such as TLS should be used, or the component should be signed using XML-Signature to prevent alteration during delivery. The RFC assumes that VTS plug-ins are trusted and installed by checked means (like other downloaded applications). It also assumes that the voucher itself (the instance, not the component template) includes a unique serial number or similar mechanism to prevent duplication and forgery, usually outside the Voucher Component itself.
sections.eli5: Vouchers need to be kept secure so nobody can forge them or use them twice. The voucher system provider and the issuer both need to be trustworthy.
